title: My Visit to Alpha School: Part 1
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler reports from a tour of Alpha School's flagship campus in Austin, aiming to add first-hand observation to a controversy that has split even the science of learning community. She explains that Alpha's leaders claim pupils learn twice as fast in two hours of app-based morning instruction, with adult guides rather than teachers, while critics such as Daniel Willingham doubt that compressing learning in this way preserves breadth and depth. Most critics, she notes, have not visited, and she sets out to give a more complicated picture than either side has offered. In her visit she saw K-1 pupils working with phonics and language apps, with guides roaming the room, and she was told that the model is constantly changing, especially in K-2 literacy. She is encouraged that nonfiction texts are knowledge-building and that Socratic seminars and book talks are planned, and she asks whether Alpha will begin to resemble regular school with an AI component.
points: First-hand observation shows an Alpha classroom that looks surprisingly ordinary, and Wexler argues both its boosters and critics have often worked from second-hand accounts.
Alpha is an evolving experiment, particularly in K-2 literacy, where new AlphaPhonics and AlphaLanguage apps give targeted practice that the school says makes two hours enough.
Guides who roam, encourage persistence and earn six-figure salaries are central to how the model avoids pupils floundering in front of screens.
The reading app uses knowledge-focused nonfiction texts, and planned book talks and Socratic seminars suggest the school may adapt toward shared reading with adults.
quotes: This could be almost any American kindergarten or first grade classroom, but these kids are getting a fundamentally different approach to education. That’s because they attend the flagship campus of an institution that has become the center of a lot of recent buzz and controversy: Alpha School.

Alpha’s leaders claim that students learn at least twice as fast as they would in a regular school in just two hours a day—during the morning, when instruction is delivered through screens and apps. They spend the remainder of the school day in guide-led workshops designed to teach them “life skills” like grit.

Beyond that, there’s been a serious split over Alpha within the “science of learning” community—a group of people who have been trying to communicate basic principles of cognitive science to teachers in the U.S. and several other countries for the past decade or more. Teachers rarely learn those principles during their training, and in fact often learn things that contradict them.

Most of the individuals who are critiquing Alpha haven’t been to the school, and I don’t think they’ve had the kinds of conversations I was able to have with people who work there. I’m not saying that what follows will answer every question that has been raised about Alpha, many of which are legitimate.

One problem with getting a handle on Alpha is that—as I was told repeatedly—things are constantly changing. In a way, the school has long been an ongoing experiment. If something doesn’t appear to be working, it gets changed.

In the K-1 classroom I visited, a girl sat in front of a screen displaying one-syllable words with the short “a” sound: tap, map, pat, sat, at. She tapped on a microphone icon on the screen and read each word aloud, after which the app gave her another round of words to read. Alpha’s AI appears do a good job of determining whether a child is decoding words correctly.

As for the revised version of AlphaLanguage, it’s clearly an improvement over software that foregrounds isolated comprehension skills. But what about the shared experience of reading a book, with an adult human guiding students to think and exchange ideas about the content?

But Vaites told me that Alpha will be piloting “Socratic Seminars and other ‘book talks’” at the elementary level early next year. The goal, she said, is to roll that innovation out across K-12 by the 2027-28 school year, for at least four books a year. Those discussions will take place outside of the two-hour academic block and will be led by an adult, although it’s not clear whether those will be guides or someone else.
